_meta.note: Editorial data for generated X-vs-Y pages (render_vs_pages in build.py). Pricing numbers ALWAYS come from tools.json via the engine - never write prices here. Verdict/stripNote/whyLoser are hand-written per pair (design drafts, owner approves, inserted verbatim incl. HTML).

conventions.pair order: slug 'a' = more searched tool (zapier > make > n8n > pipedream > activepieces > automatisch > node-red); page slug = '<a>-vs-<b>.html'; array order = production priority (cross-links pick nearest published pairs from the top)
conventions.winner: slug of the overall value pick from the verdict - gets the .winner outbound card
conventions.stripNote: optional tagline after the vs-strip (e.g. 'at every volume we track') - only when the winner is uniform across volumes; omit when winners flip
conventions.verdict: verbatim HTML for the hero verdict box (may contain <b class="win">)
conventions.faq: optional full FAQ override [{q, a-html}]; when absent the generator builds standard FAQs from data + whyLoser
conventions.whyLoser: editorial answer to 'Why would anyone pick <loser>, then?' - used by auto-FAQ when faq override absent

zapier.opDef: In Zapier, one task = one action step — a 3-step Zap triggered 100 times consumes 300 tasks.
zapier.ctaBlurb: 100 free tasks a month on 2-step Zaps — fine for checking whether your apps are supported.

make.opDef: In Make, one operation = one module execution, counted per module across the scenario.
make.ctaBlurb: 1,000 free ops a month, unlimited scenarios — enough to run a real pilot before paying anything.

n8n.opDef: n8n Cloud counts workflow executions — one run is one execution regardless of step count; self-hosted n8n has no metering at all.
n8n.ctaBlurb: Community Edition is free forever self-hosted; Cloud has a free trial — test a real workflow either way.

pipedream.opDef: In Pipedream, one credit ≈ 30 seconds of compute per step — a multi-step workflow typically consumes several credits per run.
pipedream.ctaBlurb: Free tier gives 100 credits a month on 3 workflows — enough to validate an integration.

activepieces.opDef: Activepieces doesn't meter runs at all — pricing is per active flow, with unlimited executions.
activepieces.ctaBlurb: 10 active flows free with unlimited runs — a real pilot costs nothing.

automatisch.opDef: Automatisch doesn't meter operations — one flat cloud price, or self-host for free.
automatisch.ctaBlurb: Open source — self-host for free, or take the flat-price cloud plan.

node-red.opDef: Node-RED has no metering — it's open-source software you run on your own hardware.
node-red.ctaBlurb: Free and open source — install and run in minutes on a Pi or VPS.

pairs.verdict: Make is 14–24× cheaper at paid volumes — and its free tier covers 1,000 ops/mo outright; Zapier wins on integration count — 9,000+ vs 1,500+. If your apps exist in both ecosystems, Make is the value pick. If you depend on a long-tail integration only Zapier has, that decides it.
pairs.whyLoser: Integrations. With 9,000+ supported apps versus Make's 1,500+, Zapier is often the only tool that connects a niche CRM or legacy system. If the integration you need exists only there, the price premium is the cost of admission.

faq.a: At every volume we track, yes — from $0 vs $58.50 at 1,000 ops/mo to $116.47 vs $733.50 at 100,000. Make's volume pricing scales far more gently than Zapier's per-task tiers, so the gap widens as you grow.

faq.q: What counts as an operation on each?
faq.a: In Zapier, one task = one action step — a 3-step Zap triggered 100 times consumes 300 tasks. In Make, one operation = one module execution, counted similarly per module. Both count multi-step workflows multiplicatively, so the per-unit price difference is what matters.

faq.q: Can I self-host either of them?
faq.a: No — both are cloud-only. If self-hosting matters to you (cost control, GDPR, data residency), look at n8n or Activepieces instead — see the compare tool.

faq.q: Why would anyone pick Zapier, then?
faq.a: Integrations. With 9,000+ supported apps versus Make's 1,500+, Zapier is often the only tool that connects a niche CRM or legacy system. If the integration you need exists only there, the price premium is the cost of admission.
Taken from official pricing pages and verified June 2026. Values marked ~ are estimates for custom enterprise tiers. Every change we record lands in the price changelog.

pairs.stripNote: at every volume we track — self-hosted
pairs.verdict: n8n self-hosted is the cheaper option at every volume we track — but only if you self-host it; Zapier is the no-code path with 9,000+ integrations. n8n's Community Edition software is free; you pay only for the server, which scales from ~$8/mo on a small VPS up to ~$66/mo for high volume — hardware, not a tool fee. If nobody on your team wants to own a server, compare against n8n Cloud ($24–60/mo at low volume) instead: still cheaper than Zapier's $73–$733 across the same range, but no longer a rout.
pairs.whyLoser: Because n8n's low price assumes you run it yourself — installing, updating, backing up and monitoring your own server, whose cost grows with volume ($8–66/mo). If that's not your team, the realistic alternative is n8n Cloud at $20–50/mo with execution quotas. Zapier's no-code editor and 9,000+ integrations mean a non-technical person can build and own automations without engineering — that convenience is what the premium buys.

pairs.verdict: Price barely separates these two — Make's free tier wins at 1,000 ops, n8n self-hosted (from ~$8/mo) wins above it, and at 5,000 ops the gap is roughly a dollar. The real decision is whether you want to run a server: happy to self-host → n8n; want a managed cloud with a visual builder → Make. Either way, you won't overpay by much.
pairs.whyLoser: Because self-hosting isn't free in practice — n8n runs on a VPS you patch, back up and monitor yourself, and its cost climbs with volume ($8–66/mo). Make is fully managed, its free tier covers 1,000 ops/mo outright, and even at 100,000 ops it's ~$45/mo. If nobody on the team wants server keys, Make is the sane default — you're paying a few dollars for zero ops burden.

pairs.verdict: Pipedream is roughly 3–4× cheaper at every volume we track; the catch is who it's built for — Pipedream is code-first (Node/Python steps), Zapier is no-code. If your team writes code, Pipedream gives you more power for a fraction of the price. If "add a code step" sounds like a blocker, Zapier's 9,000+ integrations and point-and-click editor are what you're paying for.
pairs.whyLoser: Because Pipedream's price assumes someone on the team is comfortable in code — workflows lean on Node/Python steps and the whole UI is aimed at developers. With Zapier, a marketer or ops person can ship an automation alone: no-code editor, 9,000+ integrations, huge template library. If that's who's building, Zapier earns its premium.

pairs.stripNote: at every volume we track — up to 10 active flows
pairs.verdict: Activepieces Cloud runs this at $0 — unlimited runs, free up to 10 active flows (we price 3); n8n is the deeper toolkit once automations get complex. Both are open-source and self-hostable, so philosophy doesn't decide this one: start free on Activepieces if 10 flows is enough, move to n8n (self-hosted from ~$8/mo, scaling with volume) when you need its bigger node ecosystem and heavier workflow logic.
pairs.whyLoser: Because the $0 has a ceiling: 10 active flows on Activepieces Cloud, then $5 per extra flow. n8n self-hosted has no workflow cap — you pay only for the server (from ~$8/mo, more at high volume) — and its larger ecosystem and more mature advanced logic (branching, error handling, code nodes) start to matter once automations get serious. Heavy or complex usage tips the math back to n8n.

pairs.stripNote: at every volume we track — up to 10 active flows
pairs.verdict: Activepieces runs this at $0 at every volume — free up to 10 active flows (we price 3), then $5 per flow; Zapier's case is its catalog — 9,000+ integrations vs 747+. If your apps are covered in Activepieces' smaller catalog, the price gap ($0 vs $58–$733) is impossible to argue with. If they aren't, no discount fixes a missing integration.
pairs.whyLoser: Because 747+ integrations covers the popular apps, not the long tail — Zapier's 9,000+ catalog is the deepest in the market, and if your workflow depends on a niche CRM or a regional tool, Zapier is often the only one that has it. Add the most mature template library and a no-code editor honed for non-technical users, and the premium buys certainty that your stack is supported.

pairs.verdict: Make is 5–9× cheaper at every volume we track — and this time the no-code tool is the cheap one; Pipedream is the developer's pick. Make's free tier covers 1,000 ops/mo outright and even 100,000 ops runs ~$45 vs ~$400. Choose Pipedream only if your team wants to write Node or Python steps — then the premium buys real programmability.
pairs.whyLoser: Because Pipedream is built for engineers: workflows are code steps in Node or Python with full access to npm and PyPI packages, an event-data inspector, and 2,000+ integrations behind an API-first design. Make's visual builder hits a ceiling when logic gets genuinely complex — at that point Pipedream's premium is buying capability Make simply doesn't have.

pairs.verdict: Both start at $0 for light usage — at 1,000 ops/mo it's a dead heat; above that, Activepieces stays free while Make starts charging — though never much ($9 to ~$45/mo). The trade: Activepieces is open-source and self-hostable but free only up to 10 active flows (we price 3); Make has the bigger catalog (1,500+ integrations vs 747+) and the more mature cloud. Pick by catalog coverage first — at these prices, money is the tiebreaker, not the decider.
pairs.whyLoser: Because Make's costs are modest and predictable while its platform is the more mature one — a bigger integration catalog (1,500+ vs 747+), a more polished scenario builder, and a larger template and community pool. Activepieces' $0 also has a ceiling: 10 active flows, then $5 per flow. A growing team can outgrow it — and at $9–~$45/mo, Make was never a budget risk to begin with.

pairs.stripNote: at every volume we track — self-hosted
pairs.verdict: n8n self-hosted is cheaper at every volume we track — if you run it yourself; Pipedream is the managed path for the same developer audience. This isn't no-code vs code — both are dev-friendly. It's your server + open-source vs managed cloud + code steps: if running a VPS is routine for your team, n8n wins on price outright (a server bill of ~$8–66/mo vs Pipedream's $29–~$400+). If you'd rather never touch infrastructure, Pipedream's premium is the hosting bill.
pairs.whyLoser: Because n8n's low price assumes you operate it yourself — the server bill scales with volume ($8–66/mo) and n8n Cloud, the managed alternative, runs $20–50/mo with execution quotas. Pipedream is fully managed, scales without your attention, and its code-step model (Node/Python, npm/PyPI) is arguably the more powerful developer experience. Teams that count engineering hours often find Pipedream's fee cheaper than owning a server.
